question_en: How do I write a simple safety plan (SOP) for my village experience? I am not educated in tourism.
answer: Make one page for each activity. Keep it short enough to read in two minutes. A good page has: what the activity is, who leads it, how many guests, what can go wrong, what you do if it does, and who to call.
actions: Write the activity name, the leader, the helper, the group size you allow and the start and end time at the top of one page.
List three to five things that could hurt someone (for example slipping, heat, animals, fire, tools) and write one control for each.
Add a short emergency box with the nearest clinic, a vehicle owner, a ward member and the police or forest contact, then test the numbers every season.
caution: This is a method, not a legal form. Some states and activities have their own safety rules. Ask the District Tourism Office what applies to you.
evidence: S182 states tourist safety is mainly a State subject, so local rules matter. The one-page layout is general good practice.
verify_with: District Tourism Office; local doctor or health worker

question_en: What should I tell guests before we start an activity? I forget things when I speak.
answer: Give a short briefing in the language the guests understand, before every activity, even for regular guests. Cover what the activity is, the risks, what to wear or carry, what to avoid, and what the signals and emergency steps are. Let guests ask questions and say if they have health problems.
actions: Use a written card with five points: what we will do, what can go wrong, rules for today, how to stop me, and what we do in an emergency.
Show one thing by hand, for example how to hold a tool or how to walk on a slope, instead of only talking.
Ask each guest quietly about health problems, allergies, medicines and fears, and note the answers on your list.
caution: Do not rush the briefing when guests are tired or excited. If a guest cannot follow the language, use pictures or a helper who can translate.
evidence: S181 (Andhra Pradesh adventure rules) says the briefing should cover the nature and risks of the activity, protective gear, do's and don'ts, and emergency signals and steps, in a language participants understand. Other states may differ.
verify_with: District Tourism Office; your state adventure rules if any

question_en: When should I cancel or stop an activity? I do not want to lose the guests, but I am afraid of accidents.
answer: Decide your stop rules in advance, write them on your SOP page, and let any one leader stop the activity. Common triggers are bad weather, rising water, a sick or hurt person, coming darkness, a missing guide, or a guest who is drunk or unwell. Cancelling early costs less than a rescue.
actions: List five or six clear stop rules, for example no start in heavy rain or rising river, and tell guests at booking time.
Agree who can say stop (the lead and the helper) and promise nobody will be blamed for stopping.
Offer a refund, a new day or a safe indoor activity so you are not pushed to continue.
caution: The exact limits (rain, wind, river level) depend on your place. Ask older villagers, local rescue or forest staff, and check the weather forecast.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: District Tourism Office / local expert

question_en: Who should be in charge during an activity, and how many helpers do I need?
answer: Name one lead who makes the decisions and one helper who walks at the back and counts guests. Add specialists if the activity needs them (cook, boatman, climbing guide). The right number depends on the activity, the terrain and the guests, so decide it with your risk list and not by habit.
actions: Write each person's job on the SOP page: lead, back helper, first-aid person, driver or contact person.
Count guests at the start, at every stop and at the end, and say the number aloud.
Train one more person as a backup so the activity is not led by the only expert when they are sick.
caution: For adventure activities, some states ask for certified guides and first-aid training. Check your state rules before you advertise the activity.
scope: India (general practice); example from Andhra Pradesh
evidence: S181 (Andhra Pradesh) asks for activity-specific guide certification and first aid/CPR for guides and operators. This is one state's rule, shown as an example.
verify_with: District Tourism Office; state tourism department

question_en: What should we do after the guests leave? Is feedback really needed?
answer: Yes, a short close is part of the activity. Count the tools, clear waste, check the site for fire, spills and litter, and ask guests two or three simple questions. Write one thing to fix next time. This protects your place and improves your next group.
actions: Collect all waste and take it to the correct bin or compost; do not leave it for the village to deal with.
Check that fire is fully out, tools are locked away and animals and gates are secure.
Ask guests what felt safe, what felt confusing and what they would change, then write the answers in a notebook.
caution: If anyone was hurt, even slightly, write what happened the same day and discuss it with your group.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Your community group or trainer

question_en: Do I need permission or a licence to offer trekking, rafting or camping to guests?
answer: Tourist safety is mainly a State matter in India, so the rules and permits for trekking, camping and water sports depend on your state, and also on forest, river and land rules. The Ministry of Tourism has sent Model Adventure Safety Guidelines to all States and Union Territories for adoption, so your state may have a newer rule. Do not start such an activity for paying guests before you check.
actions: Ask the District Tourism Office in writing which adventure rules, registration and insurance apply to your activity.
Ask the Forest Range Officer or the local authority whether the trail, river or camp site needs permission.
Keep the reply or permit in a file and show it to partners and guests.
caution: Rules and fees differ by state and change. Do not copy another state's rule. See the legal and licensing rows for permits and insurance details.
evidence: S180: MoT circulated Model Adventure Safety Guidelines to States/UTs. S182 (16 Mar 2026): safety of tourists is essentially a State subject. S181: one state example (Andhra Pradesh G.O. 2025 with registration, insurance and guide norms). Full model text not read.
verify_with: District Tourism Office; Forest department; state adventure tourism authority

question_en: How do I find the dangers in my activity before an accident happens?
answer: Do a walk-through of the whole activity with a helper, step by step, as if you were a first-time guest. At each step ask: what could hurt someone, how likely is it, and what is the simple fix. Fix the big ones first and redo the walk-through each season.
actions: Walk the full route or workspace once, with a notebook, and note slippery, sharp, hot, deep or crowded places.
Mark each problem as fix now, fix before guests come, or avoid by changing the plan.
Include children, older people and people with disabilities in your thinking, since they face different risks.
caution: A checklist does not replace good judgement on the day. Use the stop rules.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Local trainer or tourism office

question_en: Should I ask guests about health problems? Is it okay to refuse someone?
answer: Yes. Ask each guest to tell you about conditions that matter for the activity, such as heart or breathing problems, pregnancy, diabetes, allergies, recent surgery or fear of heights or water. Ask in a private and polite way. If the activity is too risky for someone, offer a gentler role or alternative, and do not shame them.
actions: Use a short form or a spoken checklist asking about health issues, medicines and allergies before activities like walking, farm work, water or cooking.
Keep the answers private and share only what the first-aid person needs.
Offer an alternative such as watching, cooking, or a short walk when you must say no.
caution: You are not a doctor. Do not give medical advice or promise safety. Suggest guests to speak to their own doctor if worried.
evidence: S181 (Andhra Pradesh) says participants must declare pre-existing medical conditions before adventure activities. Asking is general good practice for all activities.
verify_with: Local doctor or health worker

question_en: What first-aid items should I carry on walks and activities, and who should know how to use them?
answer: Carry a basic first-aid kit on every activity and make sure at least one person has done a recognised first-aid course. Check the kit each month for expired items. Some state adventure rules ask for first aid and CPR training for guides, so ask yours.
actions: Ask the local Red Cross branch, health centre or an NGO about a first-aid course for your hosts and guides.
Check the kit before each trip and replace used or expired items.
Put the nearest clinic or hospital and the transport plan on your SOP page.
caution: A kit is not treatment. For serious injury or illness, move to the nearest medical help quickly and call the local emergency services.
scope: India (general practice); example from Andhra Pradesh
evidence: S181 (Andhra Pradesh): first aid and CPR certification mandatory for instructors, guides and operators; at least one CPR-trained person with first-aid kit at the location. Kit contents here are general practice; ask a health worker.
verify_with: District health office / Red Cross branch

question_en: What should be in an emergency plan, and who do I tell first if somebody is badly hurt?
answer: Your emergency plan needs four things: who is in charge, who gives first aid, how to reach the nearest clinic or hospital, and who to phone. Write the phone numbers, the road or path to the hospital, and where phone signal works. Practice it once with your team.
actions: Make the plan a half-page with names, numbers and a simple map of the way to the clinic.
Check mobile signal along your route and note the places where there is none.
Keep a vehicle owner and a boat or tractor owner on call for the season and agree how they will be paid.
caution: Never keep the injured person waiting to find the right person. If in doubt, call emergency services first, then your group.
scope: India (general practice); example from Andhra Pradesh
evidence: S181 (Andhra Pradesh) requires a documented emergency action plan with contact numbers, evacuation routes and roles, and reliable communication in remote areas. Presented here as a good-practice example.
verify_with: District Disaster Management Authority / Tourism Office

question_en: If a guest gets hurt in my activity, am I responsible? Should I have insurance?
answer: You may be held responsible if a guest is hurt because of poor preparation. Insurance can help but rules and products differ. Some state adventure rules ask operators for liability and accident cover. Ask your tourism office and an insurance agent what suits your activity.
actions: Ask the District Tourism Office whether insurance is required for your activity in your state.
Ask a licensed insurance agent for a quote and read what is not covered.
Keep your SOP, briefing record and guest forms; they show you took care.
caution: This is general information, not legal or insurance advice. See the legal and finance rows for details.
evidence: S181 (Andhra Pradesh) lists minimum liability and personal accident cover for adventure operators. This does not apply to other states unless they say so.
verify_with: Licensed insurance agent; District Tourism Office; a lawyer for legal questions

question_en: How do I share the money fairly with the villagers who help in an activity?
answer: Agree before the activity on who gets what, and write it down. Include everyone who does a job: the lead, the cook, the farmer, the artist, the driver and the community fund if any. Pay on time and share the price list with the group. Do not keep helpers on unpaid work as 'guests experience'.
actions: Make a simple sheet with every job in the activity and the amount or share decided by the group.
Set aside a small share for the village fund or common need only if the community agrees.
Review the sheet every season and write down changes in front of everyone.
caution: Do not copy numbers from other places. Costs and local wages differ.
evidence: S188 encourages community involvement, local youth as guides and women's self-help groups in running rural tourism. The sharing method is general practice.
verify_with: Community group / panchayat / local NGO or SHG federation

question_en: How many guests can I take in one group? Is there an official number?
answer: There is no single number for every activity. The safe size depends on the place, the activity, the guide skill and the guests' age and fitness. Some states set numbers for particular activities, and protected areas set their own. Start small, keep a guide-to-guest balance you can really manage, and increase only after you have run it safely.
actions: Ask the District Tourism Office or Forest Range Officer if a limit already exists for your place.
Test your activity with a small group first and note where you felt overstretched.
Write the limit on your SOP and refuse extra guests, even from a big booking.
caution: Do not use a number from a blog or other state as an official limit. Check locally.
evidence: S182: safety is a State subject, so limits differ by state. The test-small method is general practice.
verify_with: District Tourism Office; Forest department

question_en: Can I take tourists to my farm for sowing, harvest or a farm walk? What do I need to think about?
answer: Yes, many families offer farm visits, but plan them like a small event. Choose tasks that are safe for beginners, keep guests away from machines and chemicals, give clear hours, and tell guests that this is real work. Ask the Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or farm department if they have advice for visitors.
actions: Pick two or three simple tasks for guests, for example picking, planting seedlings or feeding animals.
Fence or mark off areas for tractors, pesticides, wells, pits and storage.
Tell guests to wear covered shoes, hat and water, and show them where the toilet and handwash point are.
caution: Pesticide spraying, ponds, wells, machines and bulls are not for guests. Do not let guests in a field soon after spraying.
evidence: S187 (Kerala RT) shows community-run village visits with paddy and farm walks. Safety method is general good practice for farm visits; US extension checklists use the same ideas, but no Indian official farm-visit norm was found.
verify_with: Nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) / District Agriculture Office

question_en: We use pesticides and fertiliser on the farm. How do I keep guests safe?
answer: Keep guests out of fields during and after spraying. Lock all chemicals away, in labelled containers, out of reach of children. Do not wash spray equipment or containers where guests walk or where animals drink. Tell guests honestly if the farm uses chemicals, and never use the word organic unless you have a recognised certificate.
actions: Schedule spraying when no guests are on the farm and keep a gap before visits, as advised by your local KVK or agriculture officer.
Store chemicals locked and away from kitchen, wells and children's play areas.
Show guests the safe walking route and mark restricted parcels with a sign or rope.
caution: Do not say 'organic' or 'chemical free' unless it is true and certified. Re-entry gaps differ by chemical; follow the label and local advice.
evidence: No Indian visitor-specific rule was verified; method is general practice.
verify_with: KVK / District Agriculture Officer; label of the product

question_en: Is it safe to give guests rides on a tractor or bullock cart? Can I charge for them?
answer: Rides can be a highlight, but a tractor, trolley or cart is a work vehicle, not made for passengers. Hurt guests may become your responsibility. Keep to slow speeds on flat, known tracks, use a trained driver, seat guests safely, and do not carry children or elders unsupervised. Check licence, insurance and road rules for carrying passengers for money.
actions: Use only a trained, sober driver, on a short flat track, away from public roads and slopes.
Give each guest a safe seat, no standing and no sitting on mudguards, and tell them to hold on.
Ask the District Transport Office whether carrying paying guests in an agricultural vehicle is allowed.
caution: Do not run rides in the rain, at night or over ponds and canals. Local transport rules apply; see the legal domain.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Regional Transport Office (RTO); District Tourism Office

question_en: Guests want to milk cows or touch farm animals. How do I make it safe and clean?
answer: Let guests help only with calm, familiar animals and with you holding the animal. Wash hands before and after contact. Keep children from kissing animals or putting hands in the mouth. Keep sick animals and those with new calves away from guests. Do not offer raw milk to guests.
actions: Choose one calm animal, keep it tied, and stand beside the guest during milking.
Provide soap and water or a handwash point right at the exit of the animal area.
Tell guests not to eat or drink in the animal area and not to touch their face.
caution: Animals can kick, bite or carry germs. Those who are pregnant, have weak immunity or are very young need extra care. For zoonotic disease questions talk to the local vet or health officer.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Local veterinary officer / animal husbandry department; district health officer

question_en: Can I show guests our beehives or a fishing pond? What if someone has a sting allergy or falls in the water?
answer: Ask guests first about bee sting allergy and swimming ability. Guests watch hives from a distance with a bee-keeper wearing protective gear. For ponds and canals, use a fenced or marked safe area, keep children within arm's reach, and do not allow swimming. Do not offer the activity if a person has severe sting allergy and no emergency medicine.
actions: Ask every guest about sting allergies and breathing problems before the hive visit.
Mark a clear viewing point, and keep guests out of bees' flight path.
Keep a rope or pole near the pond and assign an adult to watch it, and do not use boats without life jackets.
caution: Allergic reactions and drowning are serious. Get urgent medical help right away and do not wait.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Local doctor; Fisheries department; beekeeping extension officer

question_en: Families bring small children to the farm. What do I need to keep them safe?
answer: Treat the farm like a playground with hidden dangers. Tell parents that they must stay with children at all times. Cover or fence wells, tanks, pits and drains. Keep tools, chemicals and machines locked. Show children where to touch and where not to go, and give them tasks that are small and safe.
actions: Walk the farm at a child's height and fix or block any open well, tank, pit or electric wire.
Give parents a short rule card at arrival and repeat it in the language they understand.
Plan child-friendly tasks such as picking vegetables, feeding hens or planting seeds.
caution: Water bodies and machines are the biggest worries for young children. Do not leave any child unobserved.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Local health worker / Anganwadi worker for child safety advice

question_en: Guests join harvest and we feel they should pay for it. Is it okay that I also use guests as free labour?
answer: Do not rely on guests to finish farm work. Guests are there to learn, not to do your job. Charge for the experience, pay farm workers fairly, and keep real work separate. If guests want to help, let them join for a limited time and tell them honestly that it is a taste of farm life.
actions: Set a fixed time block for guest participation, for example one short session, and keep experienced workers doing the heavy work.
Pay local workers and helpers for their time, even if guests join.
Tell guests clearly what they are paying for and where the money goes.
caution: Check local labour rules if you hire workers; see the legal rows.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Community group / local NGO

question_en: We have a small tea, coffee or spice plot. Can we show it to tourists, and how do we keep it respectful for the workers?
answer: Yes, many small growers do this. Ask workers if they are comfortable with visitors and do not photograph them without permission. Keep guests on marked paths, tell them about plants, picking and drying in your own words, and do not claim certification you do not have. If you are part of a bigger estate, ask the owner first.
actions: Plan a short walk with two or three stops, such as plucking, drying and tasting, and keep it simple.
Ask workers if they agree to be seen, and offer to pay or share profits with those who show their work.
Tell guests about local plant health and harvest times honestly, without inventing history.
caution: Do not allow guests to taste unwashed leaves or berries; some plants are harmful. Estates may have separate labour and permission rules.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Estate owner; Tea/Coffee/Spices Board office for local rules

question_en: Guests want to cook with us in our kitchen. How do I keep it clean and safe?
answer: Treat the cooking class like serving food. Wash hands first, keep guests' hair tied, use clean water and clean tools, and keep raw and cooked food apart. Keep sick people out of the kitchen, including your own family. Assign one staff member to watch the hygiene and step in when needed.
actions: Set up a handwash point with soap and clean water before the class begins.
Use separate boards and knives for raw and cooked items, and cook meat and eggs fully.
Keep pets, children and smoke away from the food area.
caution: For licences, registration and food safety rules for guests, see the food-safety rows. Rules differ by what and how much you serve.
evidence: S188 says guests shall be served safe drinking water and staff must keep personal hygiene. Class-specific hygiene steps are general practice.
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer (FSSAI)

question_en: A guest says they are allergic to peanuts or cannot eat some foods. How should I handle this in a cooking class?
answer: Ask all guests before the class about allergies and food limits, such as nuts, milk, gluten, egg, fish, or faith-based diets. If you cannot make the dish safe, say so and give another dish. Keep the allergic person's food and tools separate and wash everything well. Never guess about an allergy.
actions: Ask about allergies and diets at booking and again at the start of the class, and write them down.
Use fresh clean utensils and a clean surface for the allergy-safe dish, and serve it first.
Tell guests which common allergens (nuts, milk, egg, wheat, mustard, sesame) are in each dish.
caution: A serious allergy can be life-threatening. If a person has trouble breathing or swelling, call emergency help immediately.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Local doctor; FSSAI guidance on allergens via District Food Safety Officer

question_en: Guests want to cook on our chulha. How do I stop burns and smoke problems?
answer: Keep guests at a safe distance, with one person near the fire at all times. Use a stable stool and a long-handled spoon. Keep children and loose clothes away. Ventilate the smoke as far as you can, and provide a short, comfortable cook session. Keep a bucket of water or sand nearby, and keep a burn first-aid plan.
actions: Set a clear 'cook zone' marked on the floor and let only one or two guests near the fire at a time.
Keep a bucket of water or sand, and a wet cloth, within reach before lighting.
Cool any burn under clean running water and seek medical help for anything serious.
caution: Smoke can affect asthma and eyes. Offer an alternative, such as a gas or induction demo, for people who cannot be in smoke.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Local fire service / health worker

question_en: I want to take guests on a food trail through the market and to street stalls. How do I do it without making vendors uncomfortable or guests sick?
answer: Talk to the vendors before you bring guests. Agree on timing, how many guests, and whether they will be paid for tasting or time. Choose clean, busy stalls with fresh food and safe water, and warn guests about foods they may not be used to. Do not photograph vendors without asking.
actions: Meet each vendor and agree on how guests will buy, taste and pay, and how the vendor benefits.
Choose stalls that cook food fresh and serve hot items, and tell guests to wash hands before eating.
Keep the group small enough that the lane or stall is not blocked.
caution: Do not promise food safety standards you cannot check. Guests with weak stomachs or allergies should pick carefully.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Market committee; local health officer

question_en: Can we take guests to pick wild greens, mushrooms or fruits? Is that safe and allowed?
answer: Be careful. Many wild plants and mushrooms are poisonous or look like safe ones. Forests may have rules on collecting. Only pick with people who know the species well, and never let guests pick or eat on their own. In forest land, ask the Forest Department first. Do not offer mushrooms or unknown wild items to guests.
actions: Ask the Forest Range Officer or the Forest Rights Committee if collecting is allowed for you and for guests.
Let an expert elder point out safe items, and let guests watch and smell, not pick, unless that person agrees.
Never serve wild foods that are not well known to the cook.
caution: Wrong identification of mushrooms or plants can cause serious illness or death. Do not take guests to protected areas for collection.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Forest department; local elder knowledge holders; community forest committee

question_en: Can I teach guests to make pickle or preserve food and let them take it home?
answer: Teaching is fine, but selling or giving packed food to take home can need food licences or labelling. Use clean jars and hands, and tell guests it is for their own use if you do not have a licence. Do not let them carry food that can spoil in the heat. For legal rules on packed food, check with the food-safety authority.
actions: Give guests a small sample to make and use only clean, dry containers.
Ask the District Food Safety Officer whether selling or giving take-home packs needs registration.
Write the date and ingredients on any jar they take, and tell them how to store it.
caution: Pickles and jams can still go bad or cause allergic reaction. See the food-safety domain for FSSAI licence details.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer (FSSAI)

question_en: We want to show guests how we make ghee, paneer or curd. Is it safe, and can we serve the products?
answer: A dairy class can be safe if milk is boiled and handled cleanly. Use clean vessels, wash hands, and keep the milk cold or hot, not warm. Do not serve raw milk to guests. Selling or serving dairy products regularly can need food licensing; see the food-safety rows and ask your local food safety officer.
actions: Boil milk before using it in classes and keep tools and vessels washed with clean water.
Keep ghee, curd or paneer from the class separate from products that you plan to sell until you confirm licensing.
Tell guests about milk allergy or lactose problems before they taste.
caution: Dairy goes bad quickly in heat. Throw away anything with a doubtful smell or taste.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer (FSSAI); animal husbandry office

question_en: Guests want to try pottery, weaving or woodwork. How do I keep them from getting hurt?
answer: Give guests the safest part of the craft, with you or the artisan beside them. Keep sharp tools, hot kilns, dyes and machines for the artisan. Provide aprons or gloves where needed, and good light and seating. Limit the number of guests so the artisan can watch everyone.
actions: Choose one simple task per guest, such as shaping a small pot or weaving a short length, and keep dangerous steps for the artisan.
Check tools and the floor before each session and remove broken or very sharp tools.
Keep a first-aid kit and clean water in the workshop.
caution: Dust, kiln heat, fumes and blades are risks for guests with asthma, young children and pregnant women. Ask about this before the class.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Local artisan guild; DC (Handicrafts) regional office; first-aid trainer

question_en: We use dyes, glues and polishes in our craft. Is it safe for guests to touch or breathe them?
answer: Treat dyes and chemicals as hazards. Keep guests away from hot dye baths and strong chemicals. Use gloves, ventilation and clean water. Store chemicals in labelled containers away from food and children. Do not call a dye 'natural' unless it truly is.
actions: Use the safest option guests can try, for example a cold, mild dye in a small tray, with gloves and an apron.
Keep dye waste out of drinking water sources, fields and drains, and ask local pollution officials how to dispose of it.
Tell guests plainly what the dye or paint is and whether it may stain skin or clothes.
caution: Some dyes and chemicals can cause skin or breathing problems. If a guest has a reaction, wash with clean water and get medical help.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: State Pollution Control Board; local health worker

question_en: Can I call my product handmade or traditional if I use some machine-made material? What should I tell guests?
answer: Be honest. Tell guests what part is made by hand, what is made by machine, and where materials come from. Do not call something handmade, local or traditional if it was made elsewhere or by machine. Guests trust honest explanations. There may be labels, GI or handloom marks that need official rules, so check before using them.
actions: Write a short card for each product that says who made it, where, and what is hand-done or machine-done.
Do not sell items bought from elsewhere as made in your village.
Ask the nearest handicrafts or handloom office about any official mark or label before using it.
caution: Misleading labels may be a legal and trust problem. This is not legal advice; see the legal rows.
evidence: S184 describes Pehchan ID cards and support for artisans via the Development Commissioner (Handicrafts) but does not cover labelling. Labelling method is general practice.
verify_with: Development Commissioner (Handicrafts) regional office; Handloom office; a lawyer

question_en: Guests photograph our designs and may copy them. How do I protect our patterns and name the maker properly?
answer: You cannot stop all copying, but you can reduce harm. Name the artisan or group on products, agree as a community what designs can be shown or taught, and keep sacred or clan designs for the community only. Some crafts have a GI (Geographical Indication) tag. Ask the nearest handicrafts office or an IP help centre what protection you may use.
actions: Hold a group meeting to agree which designs, motifs and techniques are open to guests and which are not.
Put the maker's or group's name and village on the products and the display.
Ask an IP or handicrafts office whether your craft can have a GI tag or other protection.
caution: Be honest with guests about what can and cannot be photographed or copied. This is general information, not legal advice.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Development Commissioner (Handicrafts); State GI/IP help centre; a lawyer

question_en: Guests keep photographing the artisans without asking. How do I handle that politely?
answer: Set the rule before the session: ask first, always. Let each artisan decide, and let them say no. Tell guests not to photograph elders, women or children without permission and not to post people's faces online if they do not want that. Offer a good photo spot or a staged moment if someone wants it.
actions: Tell guests at the start that they must ask before photographing a person or their work.
Put a small sign in the workshop in simple words and pictures.
Agree with the artisans whether guests can post or share photos and under what name.
caution: Some places and people do not allow photos at all, especially sacred or private spaces. Respect that.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Artisan group

question_en: How do I make sure the real maker, not just the middleman, gets paid when guests buy crafts?
answer: Pay the maker clearly and on time, and tell guests who gets the money. Agree on a price with the maker, add the host's share openly, and do not push prices down for guest discounts. Register artisans for government support where they qualify, such as the Pehchan ID card.
actions: Set the price with the artisan and write the maker's share and host's share on a sheet.
Pay the maker the same day or on a fixed day, and keep a payment record.
Help artisans apply for the Pehchan ID card or other schemes through the nearest handicrafts office.
caution: Scheme benefits change. Ask the handicrafts office for the current version.
evidence: S184 (6 Apr 2022): Pehchan ID cards (launched 2016) give artisans an identity to reach schemes via the Development Commissioner (Handicrafts). Details may have changed.
verify_with: Development Commissioner (Handicrafts) regional office

question_en: How do I plan a good and safe village walk for guests?
answer: Walk the route yourself first and time it. Pick stops that the owners are happy to show, with a rest point, water and a toilet. Avoid private courtyards, sacred spots and busy roads unless you have permission. Keep the walk short enough for slow walkers, and plan a quiet alternative for rain or heat.
actions: Walk the route with an elder and a youth guide and note slippery, dark, dog-prone or crowded parts.
Ask each household or shop on the route whether they agree to be on the walk and what they would like guests to do.
Plan a short break with water, shade and a clean toilet.
caution: Do not invent history. Use stories the community agrees to share, and say 'people here say' when not sure.
evidence: S187 and S188 show community-run village visits and training of local youth as guides. The route method is general practice.
verify_with: Panchayat; local heritage group

question_en: Villagers get annoyed when guests peep into houses and take photos of them. What should I tell guests?
answer: Tell guests before the walk that this is people's home, not a museum. Ask them not to enter or photograph homes, women, children and elders without permission. Keep your voice low, and do not give money or sweets to children on the lane. Ask the community what time of day suits them for walks.
actions: Give a short brief with three rules: ask first, stay on the path, no money or sweets to children.
Warn guests that the community may say no at any time and that is their right.
Tell villagers when a group is coming and how long they will stay.
caution: Giving things to children can lead to begging. Offer to support a school or community fund in a better way.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Panchayat / village committee

question_en: What should I tell guests when we visit a temple, mosque, gurudwara, church or monastery?
answer: Ask the caretaker or priest first whether visitors are welcome, at what time, and whether photography is allowed. Tell guests to dress modestly, remove shoes if required, and follow local customs for head covering, entry, and who may enter which area. Stay quiet and do not touch objects. Do not treat worship as a show.
actions: Ask the caretaker or community leader for the rules and times and note them for guests.
Brief guests before the visit and tell them it is fine to watch from outside.
Offer to leave if a ritual is in progress and do not photograph worship without permission.
caution: Rules vary by place and community. Do not assume; ask. Some spaces may be closed to non-members or to certain visitors, and that is their right.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Caretaker or religious leader of the place

question_en: Guests want to attend our festival. How do I include them without disturbing it?
answer: Ask the committee that runs the festival first. Agree on how many guests, which parts they may see and join, and where they stand. Tell guests the festival is for the community, not for them. Let community members decide about photos, dress and food. Plan for crowds, noise, and extra toilets and waste.
actions: Talk to the festival committee and write down what guests can and cannot do.
Brief guests on dress, behaviour, photos and offerings before they arrive.
Keep the group small and plan for the first-aid, toilet and waste needs.
caution: Some rituals are private or sacred. Only include them with clear permission. See the crowd rows for larger events.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Festival or village committee

question_en: Our folk artists can perform for guests. How do we do it without turning our culture into a show?
answer: Let the artists and elders decide what can be shown, when, and how. Keep the performance close to how it is done in the community, and say honestly when it is a special show and not the festival itself. Keep it short and respectful, and give the artists time to rest.
actions: Hold a meeting with artists and elders to decide which songs, dances and stories can be shared with guests.
Tell guests what the performance is, where it comes from and how to behave, using words the artists approve.
Keep shows to a length and number the artists are comfortable with.
caution: Do not invent traditions to please guests. Only share stories and customs the community agrees on.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Community elders; performing artists' group

question_en: Guests record our songs and dances and post them online. How do I get artists paid and keep control?
answer: Agree upfront with the artists what guests may record and post, and what fee they will receive. Pay before or right after the show. Ask guests not to record sacred or private songs. If a guest wants to use a recording for work or sale, ask them to get a written agreement first.
actions: Agree on a fixed fee, and who in the group gets how much, and write it down.
Tell guests at the start whether recording is allowed, and what they may or may not post.
Ask any guest who wants commercial use to speak to the group leader first.
caution: Copyright and folk-art protection are legal matters. Ask a lawyer or the cultural department if there is a serious case.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: State culture department; Sangeet Natak Akademi regional office; a lawyer

question_en: Some of our rituals and dances are sacred. Can guests watch them?
answer: Only the people who own the ritual can say yes. Many are not meant for outsiders. If the community agrees to a limited viewing, set clear rules and do not change timing for tourists. Do not treat prayers, trance or healing as entertainment, and do not photograph unless allowed.
actions: Ask the elders and ritual leaders if any part can be seen by guests, and which parts are closed.
Tell guests the rule before they come, and tell them to stay quiet and to dress as asked.
Offer a different performance that is open for guests instead.
caution: If the answer is no, respect it fully. A no is not a loss; it protects your culture.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Community elders / ritual leaders

question_en: Guests want to dance or wear our traditional dress. Is that alright?
answer: Ask the community. Many groups are happy to invite guests to a simple social dance or to try a scarf or shawl, but some dress or ornaments have a special meaning and are not for outsiders. Let hosts show how to wear it properly, and thank them. Do not rent out sacred items.
actions: Decide with the group which dances and items guests can join or try.
Brief guests on how to behave and how to wear the item respectfully.
Do not let guests sell or copy the dress or items without permission.
caution: Do not allow guests to mock or play-act the culture. If someone is uncomfortable, stop.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Community elders and artists

question_en: How close can we go to birds and nests when guiding birdwatchers?
answer: Do not go close to nests. Disturbing a nest can make parents leave, expose chicks, or draw predators. An Indian research guideline for nest observers advises keeping 12 to 15 m away, avoiding early mornings and rainy or cold days, not handling eggs or chicks, and varying paths so that no trail leads predators to the nest. Treat this as a minimum idea for guests too.
actions: Keep guests on the paths and let birds come to you; use binoculars instead of walking closer.
Tell guests not to touch nests, eggs or chicks and not to move branches for a photo.
Avoid taking guests to a known nest again and again.
caution: The guideline was written for researchers, not as a legal rule. Protected areas may have their own rules and permit conditions.
evidence: S186 (Barve et al., Indian BIRDS 16(1), 2020): at least 12-15 m from nests; avoid early mornings and bad weather; do not handle eggs/nestlings; vary routes.
verify_with: Local forest officer / birding group

question_en: Guests want to use flash or play bird calls from the phone. Is it okay?
answer: Do not use flash on birds or animals, especially at night, and do not play calls to draw them. These can stress animals and disturb nesting. Keep voices low and move slowly. Set simple rules and explain them. This is general good practice and rules inside protected areas may be stricter.
actions: Tell guests before the walk: no flash, no calls, no feeding, no chasing.
Keep groups small and quiet, and stop if an animal shows signs of stress.
Use the guide, not guests, to decide when to approach.
caution: Protected areas may ban certain gear and times. Ask the ranger.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Forest department / Range Officer

question_en: What if a guest meets a snake on the path? What should we do about snakebite?
answer: Keep guests on cleared paths, use a torch at night, wear covered shoes in grass, and never try to catch or kill a snake. If someone is bitten, keep the person calm and still, remove tight items, and get to a health facility quickly. The national plan warns against tying tourniquets, cutting, sucking and herbal remedies. Know the nearest hospital that gives anti-snake venom.
actions: Ask the nearest hospital or health centre today whether they stock anti-snake venom and write the answer on your plan.
Brief guests to stay on paths, watch their step, and tell the guide at once about any bite.
Keep a vehicle ready for the walk season so you can reach the hospital quickly.
caution: Do not delay going to hospital to try home remedies. Not all bites are venomous, but treat each as an emergency until a doctor says otherwise.
evidence: S185 (NAPSE, NCDC): harmful practices include tourniquets, cutting and suction, herbal remedies; delay and distance to a health facility drive deaths. Detailed first aid is in the National Snakebite Management Protocol (not opened).
verify_with: District Health Officer / nearest hospital

question_en: We get leeches and ticks in the rains. How do I warn and protect guests?
answer: Tell guests in advance, so they are not shocked. Suggest closed shoes, long trousers, socks and insect repellent they know is safe for them. Check skin and clothes after the walk, and remove a tick or leech carefully. Watch for fever or rash after a few days and tell guests to see a doctor if it appears.
actions: Brief guests at booking and give a simple dress list for forest and wet grass walks.
Plan a stop to check clothes and skin after the walk and keep salt-free clean water and first-aid items handy.
Tell the guest to see a doctor if fever or rash appears after the trip.
caution: Do not give medical advice. If a guest feels ill, send them to a doctor.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Local health centre

question_en: Can I lead guests into the forest or a national park for nature walks? Who do I ask?
answer: Do not take paying guests into forest or a protected area without permission from the forest department. Each protected area has its own rules about who can guide, where visitors can go, which timings and which vehicles. Core areas of tiger reserves are not open for tourists to patrol. Meet the Range Officer, ask in writing, and respect their answer.
actions: Visit or call the Range Officer and ask whether guided walks are allowed, where, with which permits and guides.
Ask whether local residents can be listed as approved guides, and how to apply.
Keep any written permission with you on every walk.
caution: Rules, entry fees and court orders change; see the law and environment rows. Do not enter without permission.
evidence: S183 (NTCA advisory, 12 Aug 2010): tourists should not be allowed to patrol core/critical tiger habitat; patrolling camps must not be used for tourism. Later NTCA guidelines and court orders may add rules; not read this session.
verify_with: Forest Range Officer / Divisional Forest Officer

question_en: We know our mountains well. Can local youth lead treks for guests, or do we need a certificate?
answer: Local knowledge is valuable, but many states also ask for guide training or registration for treks, especially for higher or risky routes. Some state examples mention courses from mountaineering institutes and first aid training. Check your state and the forest department, and treat local youth as co-guides while they train.
actions: Ask the District Tourism Office and Forest Range Officer which guide registration or training is needed for your trek.
Ask about a basic mountaineering or trekking course and a first-aid course for your youth.
Pair experienced elders and trained guides on every trek until your team is trained.
caution: Rules differ by state and route. Do not claim a person is certified unless they are.
scope: India (general practice); example from Andhra Pradesh
evidence: S181 (Andhra Pradesh): trek guides need activity-specific certification, e.g. a Basic Mountaineering Course from a recognised institute, plus first aid/CPR; fixed or permanent trek camps are not allowed there. S182: safety is a State subject.
verify_with: State tourism department; Indian Mountaineering Foundation or state mountaineering institute

question_en: The sky looks cloudy but guests want to continue the trek. When should I turn back?
answer: Set a turnaround rule before the trek, such as a time by which the group must turn back whatever the view, and clear weather signs that mean stop. Leave early, keep one buffer hour, and avoid ridges, trees and open land in lightning. The guide's decision is final. Check the weather forecast and ask locals who know the weather.
actions: Agree on a turnaround time and weather stop signs and tell guests the rule at the briefing.
Check the forecast the night before and the morning of the trek, and share the plan with a person in the village.
Turn back at the first clear stop sign, and never pressure the group to continue.
caution: Mountain and monsoon weather can change quickly. Local elders often know the signs; ask them.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Local elders; weather office forecast; mountaineering institute

question_en: We take guests above 2500 or 3000 m. What should I know about altitude sickness?
answer: Altitude sickness can happen to anyone, even fit people. Go up slowly, tell guests the signs (headache, nausea, tiredness, breathing difficulty), and never push a sick person higher. If symptoms get worse, go down and get medical help. High treks are best run by trained guides with a clear emergency plan.
actions: Brief guests on the signs of altitude sickness and ask them to tell you at once if they feel them.
Plan rest days or slow climbs, and keep water and food regular.
Descend with the person if symptoms are serious, and get medical help.
caution: Do not give medical advice or medicine. For high-altitude treks, ask a doctor and a trekking institute about your plan.
evidence: S181 (Andhra Pradesh) recommends a doctor's fitness certificate for clients on high-altitude treks. Altitude sickness method is general practice; no specific Indian norm was verified.
verify_with: Doctor with mountain experience; Indian Mountaineering Foundation / mountaineering institute

question_en: Can I set up a camp site in my field or near the forest for guests? What should I plan?
answer: Check ownership and permission first. Camping in a forest, riverbank or protected land can need permits or may be banned. In your own field, you still need safe water, toilets, waste handling, fire rules and an emergency plan. Keep sleeping tents away from rivers, steep slopes, dead trees and animal paths.
actions: Ask the landowner and the local authority whether camping is allowed at the site.
Plan toilets, safe drinking water, cooking area and waste before you take bookings.
Keep a staffed night contact and a vehicle available for emergencies.
caution: Some states do not allow permanent trek camps; check yours. Fire rules apply near forest. See law and waste domain rows.
evidence: S181 (Andhra Pradesh) says no trekking operator may set up fixed/permanent camps; other states differ. Camp planning method is general practice.
verify_with: District Tourism Office; Forest department; Gram Panchayat

question_en: Guests want to swim, kayak or use tubes in our river or pond. How do I make it safe?
answer: Water is the most dangerous part of many village experiences. Do not offer swimming or boating without trained, certified help, working life jackets, a clear safe zone and a rescue plan. Flow and depth change after rain. Never allow alcohol near water, and never leave children without an adult. Check if your state needs a licence for water activities.
actions: Walk the water site in different seasons and mark safe and unsafe zones.
Provide life jackets that fit, and a rope, a pole and a trained person with first-aid skills.
Cancel after rain, rising water or when the water is murky or fast.
caution: Many drowning cases happen in calm-looking water. Rafting and water sports often need an approved operator and licence; see your state rules.
evidence: S181 (Andhra Pradesh) requires water-activity guides to hold certification from recognised water-sports bodies and mandatory equipment inspection. Other states differ.
verify_with: District Tourism Office; State water sports / adventure authority; Irrigation department

question_en: We want to add a cycling tour, a rock climbing or a cave visit. What are the extra risks?
answer: Each adds its own hazards: traffic and falls for cycling, falls and rope failure for climbing, and dark, low air and flooding for caves. Use proper gear, a helmet for cycling and climbing, trained guides, and a small group. Do not take guests into caves or on climbs without trained people. Check whether the site is protected, and ask for permission.
actions: Test the route and the gear, and keep helmets and a repair kit for cycling.
Hire or partner with a trained climbing or caving guide before you offer these.
Skip any cave or climb if it rains, or if gear is old or doubtful.
caution: If you are not trained, do not run these on your own. Some states regulate climbing, caving and rope activities.
evidence: S181 (Andhra Pradesh) sets rules and guide requirements for ropes-based and other adventure activities, and helmet fitting for vehicle activities. Rest is general practice.
verify_with: State tourism department; mountaineering institute; Forest department

question_en: How do I decide if children or older guests can join a trek or water activity?
answer: Do not rely on age alone. Match the activity to the weakest person in the group, ask about health, and offer a shorter or easier version. Some state rules set minimum ages for specific activities; ask yours. For children, a parent or guardian must stay and sign. Be ready to say no.
actions: Ask about age, health and past experience at booking, and describe the activity clearly.
Offer an easy version, such as a shorter loop or a viewing-only role, for children and elders.
Ask your state tourism office if age limits exist for your activity.
caution: Age or fitness rules differ by activity and state. Do not copy a number from elsewhere.
evidence: S181 (Andhra Pradesh) gives age conditions for some activities (e.g. ATVs) and medical screening for rope activities. Not a national rule.
verify_with: District Tourism Office; local doctor

question_en: Should guests sign a form before an adventure activity? Does a form protect me?
answer: A short form helps record that guests understood the risks, shared health problems and agreed to the rules. It does not make you free from responsibility if you were careless. Use it with a briefing, not instead of one. Ask a lawyer to check your form.
actions: Write a simple form in plain language with the activity, risks, health questions and an emergency contact.
Read the main points aloud before signing, in the guest's language.
Keep forms safely for as long as local advice says.
caution: This is not legal advice. See the legal rows; ask a lawyer about your form.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: A lawyer; District Tourism Office

question_en: Who do we call if a guest gets lost or injured in the hills or forest?
answer: Write down the local contacts before the season: the nearest police station, health centre, forest range office, a vehicle owner, and any local rescue team or disaster response office. Ask the District Disaster Management Authority who handles rescue in your area. Practise sharing your location clearly.
actions: Collect the numbers for police, ambulance, health centre, forest range and the district disaster management office and put them on the SOP page.
Share your route and return time with someone in the village before each trek.
Check that the numbers work and signal is available along your route.
caution: Do not wait to call for help. Call early, and give the place and the number of people.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: District Disaster Management Authority; local police; Forest department

question_en: I want to offer yoga or meditation to guests. What should I be careful about?
answer: Teach only what you are trained for, and say honestly what you are. Ask guests about health problems and injuries, and offer easy options. Do not promise cure or treatment. Keep the class on clean ground with space, shade and water, and respect different beliefs and customs.
actions: Tell guests that the class is for wellbeing, not treatment, and ask about injuries, pregnancy and heart problems.
Offer easy and gentle versions of each pose and let people rest.
Say clearly who the teacher is and what training they have.
caution: Do not claim to treat or cure. If a guest has a serious health condition, advise them to ask their doctor first.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Ministry of AYUSH recognised yoga teacher bodies / a doctor; District Tourism Office

question_en: Guests ask for Ayurvedic massage or herbal treatments. Can I offer them?
answer: Be careful. Treatments, massages and herbal medicines may need qualified practitioners and permissions. Do not offer medicines or treatment unless you are qualified and allowed to. Do not claim cures. You may share traditional knowledge as a story or a demonstration if the knowledge-holders agree, without selling medicines.
actions: Ask the District AYUSH or health office what licence or qualification is needed for the service you plan.
Work with a qualified practitioner for any massage or therapy and keep them accountable for it.
Tell guests honestly that the activity is a wellbeing experience and not medical treatment.
caution: Do not promise to treat diseases. Advertising health claims has legal limits; see the legal rows.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: District AYUSH officer; State medical council or AYUSH board; a lawyer

question_en: Guests want to join a village pilgrimage walk or meditation at a holy place. How do I keep it respectful?
answer: Ask the community and the keepers of the place if guests are welcome and how. Tell guests the rules of conduct, such as dress, silence, shoes and offerings. Do not turn prayer into entertainment, and do not photograph worship without permission. Keep the walk at the pace of pilgrims and make sure water and toilets are available.
actions: Ask the temple committee or keepers whether guests may join, and when.
Brief guests on dress, behaviour and photos, and tell them it is a belief, not a show.
Plan water, rest, shade and toilets, and carry first aid, since pilgrim walks can be long and hot.
caution: Do not make claims about spiritual or health benefits. Respect those who do not want guests.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Temple or shrine committee; community elders

question_en: Guests want to visit a children's home or orphanage in our area. Should I arrange it?
answer: No. Do not arrange tourist visits to orphanages or children's homes. Visits and volunteering there can harm children and are linked to orphanage trafficking. Children need privacy, stable carers and protection. Offer guests another way to help, such as supporting a school or a community fund through proper channels.
actions: Say politely that you do not arrange orphanage or children's home visits, and explain why.
Offer a safer alternative such as a skills workshop run by qualified local adults, or a donation to a registered organisation after checking it.
Tell guests that childcare institutions have legal rules and that visits can be harmful, and ask them to follow child protection principles.
caution: If you suspect a child is in danger, contact the local Childline or child protection officer. Child protection law is detailed; see the legal rows or ask the District Child Protection Unit.
evidence: S189 (Better Care Network brief): overview of harms of orphanage volunteering, orphanage tourism and trafficking linked to it. India-specific legal rules not verified this session.
verify_with: District Child Protection Unit / Childline; a lawyer

question_en: Guests want to visit the village school and meet children. Is it okay?
answer: Only with written permission from the head teacher and the school committee, and not during class time unless they ask. Keep visits rare, short and planned by the school, not by tourists. Do not allow photos of children, gifts or one-to-one time. Let the school decide what is useful, such as a talk or a shared activity with teachers present.
actions: Ask the head teacher and the school committee if they want any visits, and under what rules.
Make a written rule that guests never take children's photos, give them sweets or gifts, or meet them alone.
Let the school suggest a useful contribution, such as books chosen by the teacher, instead of ad hoc gifts.
caution: Public school rules differ by state. Never go behind the school's decision.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Head teacher / Block Education Officer

question_en: Foreign and city volunteers want to stay and help in our village. How should I manage it?
answer: Decide what the village actually needs, and only take volunteers who bring a skill that locals have asked for. Write a short agreement with start and end dates, tasks, who supervises, fees if any, and where the money goes. Do not let volunteers replace paid local jobs. Keep volunteers away from unsupervised contact with children.
actions: Write a short list of tasks the community wants help with and who will supervise each task.
Give each volunteer a written agreement covering tasks, rules, fees, safety and what happens if they break the rules.
Review each placement with the community and stop it if it does harm or takes local jobs.
caution: Visa and legal rules for foreign volunteers are complex. Check with the district authorities and a lawyer.
evidence: S189 explains harms of unmanaged voluntourism, particularly with children. The agreement method is general practice.
verify_with: District Tourism Office; a lawyer; local police or foreigner registration office for foreign guests

question_en: How do I check that a volunteer or guest is safe around children and women?
answer: Keep it simple and fair. Ask for ID and references, talk to them in person or by video, and set clear rules on contact with children and women. Never allow one-to-one time with children. Ask the local police station what verification options exist. A check does not replace supervision.
actions: Ask each volunteer for ID, a reference and a short written agreement before they arrive.
Make a rule that a villager adult is always present when a volunteer is with children.
Ask your local police station how to request verification and what is allowed.
caution: Do not store or share people's ID papers carelessly; see the data privacy rows.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Local police station; a lawyer

question_en: Can we offer a language class or let guests teach English to our youth?
answer: Yes, if it is useful to the village and managed well. A short class where guests learn a few local words with a local teacher is a great experience, and it pays a local teacher. If guests offer to teach youth, check their skill, keep adults present, and make it a planned course, not a drop-in activity.
actions: Create a short, paid lesson for guests with a local teacher using words and phrases the community likes.
For guests who want to teach, ask first what skills the youth want and who will supervise.
Check teaching quality, and keep sessions short and in public spaces.
caution: Do not let guests replace local teachers.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Community group; local teachers

question_en: Guests want a bonfire in the evening. How do I do it safely?
answer: Choose a clear, flat spot away from houses, trees, dry grass and tents. Keep the fire small, with water or sand close by and one adult watching it at all times. Do not allow children near the fire without an adult, and put the fire out fully before sleeping. Check for local bans, especially near forests and in dry season.
actions: Mark a fire ring with stones and clear dry leaves from around it before lighting.
Keep a bucket of water or sand, and put the fire out with water and check that it is cold.
Ask the Forest Range Officer or Panchayat whether fires are allowed near forest, especially in the dry season.
caution: Forest fire rules are strict. Do not burn plastic or treated wood. See waste rows.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Forest department; Gram Panchayat; local fire service

question_en: Can I take guests out at night to look at stars or take a night walk?
answer: Yes, if the place is safe. Visit the spot in the daytime first, check for holes, water, animals and snakes, and use torches with red or low light so eyes can adjust. Keep the group small and together, and count guests. Do not take guests into forest or protected areas at night unless permitted. Protected tiger reserves have strict night rules.
actions: Check the site and path by day and remove or mark hazards.
Carry torches, a first-aid kit, a phone and extra batteries, and keep everyone together.
Ask the forest authority before you plan any night activity near forest.
caution: Night tourism is banned or restricted in many protected areas. Confirm with the forest department.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Forest department; Gram Panchayat

question_en: Guests and some villagers want alcohol at the evening programme. What should I do?
answer: Be clear and calm. Selling or serving alcohol needs a licence in India and rules differ by state. Dry states and local bans apply. Even where it is allowed, keep it away from water, fire, climbing and young people, and do not let drunk guests join activities. Ask the local excise office before any plan.
actions: Ask the excise office and the panchayat what is allowed in your village and state.
Make a house rule that no activity involving fire, water, heights or vehicles happens after drinking.
Be ready to ask a drunk guest to stop or leave, with another adult beside you.
caution: Do not sell alcohol without a licence. See the legal rows.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: State Excise Department; Gram Panchayat

question_en: How do I keep women guests and women villagers safe and comfortable at evening events?
answer: Plan for safety. Keep lighting good, keep the programme in a visible public place, and have a clear way to report problems. Walk guests back in groups, with a woman guide where possible. Tell all guests the rules: no touching, no unwanted photos, no pressuring women to dance or drink. Support the person if something happens, and call the police if needed.
actions: Light the paths and the venue, and avoid isolated spots for evening events.
Put one woman from the community and one host as contact persons for guest or villager complaints.
Brief guests on respectful behaviour and ask anyone who breaks it to leave.
caution: Take any complaint seriously and do not blame the person who reports. For serious incidents, police and women's helplines apply; see the safety and legal rows.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Local police station; Internal/Local Committee where applicable; women's helplines

question_en: Neighbours complain about loud music and bright lights from our evening programme. What should I do?
answer: Respect the neighbours. Fix an end time, keep sound low and turned away from houses, and use warm, shaded lights. Tell nearby families about events before they happen. Birds, animals, sick people and students also need quiet. Check noise rules for your area, since they differ by place.
actions: Agree an end time with the neighbours and the panchayat, and stick to it.
Use soft, low lights pointed down, and avoid loudspeakers.
Tell nearby households before every event and ask for feedback afterwards.
caution: Noise rules, especially at night and near protected areas, are legal matters; ask the local authority.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Gram Panchayat; State Pollution Control Board / local police

question_en: Thousands of pilgrims come during our festival. How do we host them without chaos?
answer: Plan with the festival committee and the panchayat. Estimate how many people the paths, toilets, water and parking can handle, and plan more toilets, waste pickup, drinking water, first aid and exits. Keep paths clear, plan one-way flow if the place is narrow, and have a plan for lost children and medical cases.
actions: Meet the festival committee, local police and health office early and ask what crowd plan exists.
Plan water points, toilets, bins and first aid, and put volunteers at key points.
Keep exit paths free and agree on a simple signal for emergency.
caution: Crowd crushes are life-threatening. Do not expect your homestay or stall to handle crowds alone; work with the authorities.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: District administration / local police / festival committee

question_en: Families want to hold weddings or parties at my farm or homestay. What should I check?
answer: Events bring crowds, noise, fire, alcohol and waste. Set a guest limit your space can handle, have enough toilets and safe water, and arrange waste and cleaning. Check permissions for loudspeakers, food and alcohol, and any rules from the panchayat. Make a written agreement on timing, damage and who is responsible.
actions: Decide the maximum number of people and tell the family before booking.
Add portable or extra toilets, handwash points and bins for the event.
Ask the panchayat and local authority about permissions for sound, food and alcohol.
caution: Rules for events and sale of food or alcohol differ by state and place. See food safety and legal rows.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Gram Panchayat; local police; District Food Safety Officer

question_en: A school or college group wants to stay with us. What extra care do I need?
answer: Talk to the teacher in charge before booking. Ask the number of students, ages, boys and girls, any health needs, and how many adults come. Plan separate and safe rooms, safe water, a clear schedule and enough staff. The teachers stay responsible for the students, and you stay responsible for your site and activities.
actions: Ask for the teacher's contact, student list, health needs and a written plan for supervision.
Plan sleeping, toilets and safety rules, and brief teachers and students together.
Keep activities simple and avoid water or adventure unless trained staff are present.
caution: Protect children and young people with clear rules and supervision. See child safety rows.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: School / college; District Tourism Office

question_en: A company wants to bring a team to work and relax at my place. What do I need to plan?
answer: Ask what the group wants: quiet rooms and Wi-Fi, or activities and meals. Check your power, internet, space and water can handle the group. Agree on dates, number of people, and what is included in writing. Plan activities that suit working people and keep them safe, and give the host and community fair pay.
actions: Ask the company about group size, schedule, activities and dietary needs.
Test your internet and power and tell them honestly about limits.
Write an agreement about price, extras, cancellation and what is not included.
caution: Do not promise Wi-Fi or comforts you cannot provide. For tax and legal questions see the finance and legal rows.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Community group; tourism trainer

question_en: How do I handle waste, water and toilets when many guests come for one event?
answer: Plan before the day. Count how many people will come, and arrange enough toilets, handwash points and safe drinking water for them. Provide labelled bins for wet and dry waste and a plan to remove it. Use steel plates and cloth bags if you can, and avoid single-use plastic. Clean up straight after the event.
actions: Estimate the crowd and arrange extra toilets and refilling water points before the day.
Place labelled bins and agree who empties them and where waste goes.
Use refill water and reusable plates, and tell guests the rules at entry.
caution: Waste and sanitation rules are legal matters; see the waste domain rows and ask your panchayat.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Gram Panchayat / Block office; district sanitation officer

question_en: How should I change my activities in the monsoon?
answer: Plan for slippery paths, flooded streams, landslide risk, mud, leeches and sudden storms. Move walks and water activities to safer times or cancel them, and offer indoor options such as cooking, crafts or stories. Check road and river status before every trip, and keep your emergency plan ready.
actions: Re-check each route and site at the start of the monsoon and mark closed or risky areas.
Add rain stop rules and indoor alternatives to your SOP pages.
Tell guests to bring rain gear, spare clothes and shoes with grip.
caution: Heavy rain, floods and landslides can strand guests. Follow the District Disaster Management Authority warnings.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: District Disaster Management Authority; weather office

question_en: How do I adjust activities for very hot summers and cold winters?
answer: In summer, move activities to early morning or evening, add shade, water and rest, and watch for heat illness. In winter, plan for cold mornings, shorter daylight, fog and warm clothing. Ask guests about health and check their clothing. Adjust the route length and timing, and cancel if the weather turns dangerous.
actions: Shift outdoor activities away from the hottest or coldest hours and shorten routes.
Provide drinking water, shade or warm drinks and tell guests what to wear.
Watch for signs of heat illness or cold stress and stop the activity if someone looks unwell.
caution: Heat and cold can be dangerous to children, elders and sick people. Keep medical help in mind.
evidence: Good-practice method for rural experiences; not a legal rule. Local rules and local knowledge come first.
verify_with: Local health centre; weather office
